plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 18: Temperature and Heat
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single pressure-temperature plot headed H2O. The vertical axis reads "Pressure, p (atm)" with ticks at 0.006, 1, and 218, and the horizontal axis reads "Temperature, T (C)" with ticks at 0, 0.01, 100, and 374, the spacing on both visibly nonlinear. Two red curves meet at a filled dot labeled "Triple point" at 0.006 atm and 0.01 degrees, with dashed guide lines running to both axes. From that dot one branch rises almost vertically and leans slightly left, while the other sweeps up and to the right, ending at a second filled dot labeled "Critical point" at 218 atm and 374 degrees; below the triple point a single curve continues toward the lower left. Italic letters mark the regions the curves carve out: s at the left, l in the wedge between the branches, and v at the right. Curved arrows tag the branches "Melting", "Boiling", and "Sublimation", and a dashed pair marks the crossing at 1 atm and 100 degrees. Locating a point against these curves tells the reader which phase water occupies there. The plot lays out the coexistence boundaries, including the leftward-leaning melting line whose negative slope means added pressure can melt ice.

interactionPlan.concept: The pressure–temperature phase diagram of water: the coexistence curves divide p–T space into solid, liquid, and vapor regions, so a substance's phase is fixed entirely by where its state point sits relative to those curves.

Horizontal axis with arrowhead labeled 'Temperature, T (°C)' with nonlinear ticks at 0, 0.01, 100, and 374
Red fusion (melting) curve: rises nearly vertically from the triple point, leaning slightly LEFT (negative slope), off the top of the plot
Red vaporization (boiling) curve: sweeps up and right from the triple point to the critical point
Red sublimation curve: continues from the triple point down and left toward the origin corner

Dashed guide lines marking the 1 atm / 100 °C crossing on the vaporization curve
Italic region labels: 's' (solid, upper-left region), 'l' (liquid, wedge between melting and boiling curves), 'v' (vapor, lower-right region)
Curved arrow annotations labeled 'Melting', 'Boiling', and 'Sublimation' pointing at the three red branches

interactions.teaches: Moving horizontally across the diagram at fixed pressure crosses coexistence curves and changes the phase — the same substance is ice, water, or steam depending only on where it lands.
interactions.label: Temperature T (°C)

interactions.teaches: Pressure alone can change the phase: raising p at fixed T can cross the melting curve (solid → liquid) or the vaporization curve (vapor → liquid).
interactions.label: Pressure p (atm)

interactions.teaches: Which transitions a substance undergoes depends on the path through p–T space: at 1 atm ice melts then boils, below the triple-point pressure ice sublimates directly to vapor, and above the critical pressure no boundary is crossed at all.

demo_steps.title: Read the map
demo_steps.narration: Three red curves carve the plane into solid (s), liquid (l), and vapor (v). The state point sits at room conditions, 25 °C and 1 atm, inside the liquid wedge — water is liquid there for no other reason than its location on this map.

demo_steps.title: Cross the boiling curve
demo_steps.narration: Slide the temperature right at 1 atm. At 100 °C the point crosses the vaporization curve and the highlighted region flips from liquid to vapor — that crossing is boiling.

demo_steps.title: The triple point
demo_steps.narration: Drop the pressure to 0.006 atm and the temperature to 0.01 °C. All three curves meet at this single dot, the one condition where ice, water, and steam coexist.

demo_steps.title: Squeeze ice into water
demo_steps.narration: Park the temperature just below 0 °C in the solid region and raise the pressure. Because water's melting curve leans LEFT, climbing vertically eventually crosses it and the label changes from solid to liquid — pressure alone melts ice.

demo_steps.title: Sublimation path
demo_steps.narration: Choose the low-pressure path, below the triple-point pressure, and heat. The point crosses only the sublimation curve: ice turns straight into vapor with no liquid stage.

demo_steps.title: Past the critical point
demo_steps.narration: Now take the supercritical path above 218 atm and heat past 374 °C. No curve is crossed — liquid and vapor merge continuously into one indistinguishable supercritical fluid.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Phase isn't a property you carry with you — it's a location: the state point's position relative to the coexistence curves decides everything, which is why water's uniquely left-leaning melting line lets pressure alone turn ice into liquid.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Single quadrant plot with arrow-tipped axes, white background, black axes and text, the three coexistence curves drawn as one continuous red stroke (~2px). Both axes are strongly nonlinear (log-like) so that 0.006, 1 and 218 atm, and 0, 0.01, 100 and 374 °C, are all comfortably separated; ticks are labeled only at those values. From the triple-point dot (low-left-center) one branch rises steeply and tilts slightly leftward toward the top of the frame (exaggerate the negative slope so it reads clearly), another sweeps up-and-right with increasing steepness to the critical-point dot at the upper right, and a third continues down-left to near the origin. Both special points are filled black dots with plain text labels beside them. Thin black dashed guides run from each special point and from the 1 atm/100 °C crossing to the axes. Italic single-letter region labels s (upper left), l (wedge between the two upper branches), v (lower right). Curved black arrows on the outside of the frame tag 'Melting' (left, pointing at the fusion curve), 'Boiling' (right, pointing at the vaporization curve), and 'Sublimation' (lower left). Interactive additions: a translucent fill tinting the currently occupied region (blue-grey for solid, blue for liquid, warm yellow for vapor, purple wash beyond the critical point), a prominent open-circle state marker with a small readout box showing T, p and the phase name, and when a heating path is selected a horizontal dashed arrow across the plot at that pressure with small tick marks and labels at each boundary crossing ('melting', 'boiling', 'sublimation', or 'no transition').

authoredContext:
The figure shows the phase diagram for water. Using the graph, if you know the pressure and temperature, you can determine the phase of water. The solid curves—boundaries between phases—indicate phase transitions, that is, temperatures and pressures at which the phases coexist. For example, the boiling point of water is 100°C at 1.00 atm. As the pressure increases, the boiling temperature rises gradually to 374°C at a pressure of 218 atm. A pressure cooker (or even a covered pot) cooks food faster than an open pot, because the water can exist as a liquid at temperatures greater than 100°C without all boiling away. (As we’ll see in the next section, liquid water conducts heat better than steam or hot air.) The boiling point curve ends at a certain point called the critical point—that is, a critical temperature, above which the liquid and gas phases cannot be distinguished; the substance is called a supercritical fluid. At sufficiently high pressure above the critical point, the gas has the density of a liquid but does not condense. Carbon dioxide, for example, is supercritical at all temperatures above 31.0°C. Critical pressure is the pressure of the critical point.

Similarly, the curve between the solid and liquid regions in the figure gives the melting temperature at various pressures. For example, the melting point is 0°C at 1.00 atm, as expected. Water has the unusual property that ice is less dense than liquid water at the melting point, so at a fixed temperature, you can change the phase from solid (ice) to liquid (water) by increasing the pressure. That is, the melting temperature of ice falls with increased pressure, as the phase diagram shows. For example, when a car is driven over snow, the increased pressure from the tires melts the snowflakes; afterwards, the water refreezes and forms an ice layer.

The phase diagram (pT graph) for water shows solid (s), liquid (l), and vapor (v) phases. At temperatures and pressure above those of the critical point, there is no distinction between liquid and vapor. Note that the axes are nonlinear and the graph is not to scale. This graph is simplified—it omits several exotic phases of ice at higher pressures. The phase diagram of water is unusual because the melting-point curve has a negative slope, showing that you can melt ice by increasing the pressure.

Graph of pressure P in atmosphere versus temperature T in degree Celsius for water. The curve starts with going up and right to a point labeled triple point. This is at 0.006 atm and 0.01 degree C. From here, the curve diverges into two branches. One goes up and left and is almost vertical. The other goes up and right. On the branch going up and right is a point at 1 atm and 100 degrees C. Further up on the same branch is a point labeled critical point. This is at 218 atm and 374 degrees C. The area to the left of the left branch is labeled solid. The area between two branches is labeled liquid. The area to the right of the right branch is labeled vapour. The curve to the lower left of the triple point is labeled sublimation, the branch to the upper left of the triple point is labeled melting, and the branch to the upper right of the triple point is labeled boiling.

discrepancies: The liquid region is filled with a light-blue wash and a white/black state-point marker is drawn — neither exists in the source, which is an unfilled line drawing; the wash dominates the default view and changes the figure's overall look.

A floating readout box ('T = 25 °C  p = 1.00 atm / Liquid (water)') sits in the middle of the liquid region at step 0, overlapping the italic 'l' region label and colliding with the 'Boiling' leader arrow.

Curve shapes show visible kinks from the piecewise axis mapping: the melting curve bends sharply near p = 1 atm and the vaporization curve has an angular break between 100 °C and the critical point, whereas the source curves are smooth.

The melting curve in the source rises to the top of the frame well left of the 218 atm gridline with a gentle left lean; in the generated figure it tilts noticeably and the solid wedge geometry near 0.01 °C is compressed compared with the source.

'Critical point' label is placed left of the dot and 'Triple point' is placed slightly differently than the source (source: label to the right/below the dot with the text broken over two lines outside the shaded area) — minor but shifts the reading order.
evaluation.notes: A recognizable and physically sound recreation of the H₂O phase diagram with an excellent set of meaningful interactions (T/p sliders, heating-path presets, animated traversal, 6-step guided demo, curve popups), weakened by an added region wash and a floating readout box that collides with the 'l' label and 'Boiling' arrow, plus visible kinks in the coexistence curves.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are sound (concept 5, interactivity 5); the issues are implementation-level — remove the added fill/floating readout overlap, reposition labels, and smooth the curve mapping kinks.

discrepancies: The fusion/melting curve leans far more strongly to the left than in the source, where it is nearly vertical with only a slight negative slope; the generated curve's top sits well inside the liquid field, shrinking the solid region's upper shape.

Default (step-0) state adds a pale blue tint over the whole liquid field and an open state-point marker at 25 °C / 1 atm — neither exists in the source, so the resting frame is not a pure drop-in replacement for the static figure.
The sublimation curve runs slightly past the lower-left corner (below the x-axis line / left of the y-axis) instead of terminating cleanly at the axis corner as in the source.

The vaporization curve in the generated figure is flatter between the triple point and 100 °C (it nearly hugs the 1 atm guide before turning up), whereas the source shows a smoother, more continuously convex rise.
'Critical point' is centered above the critical dot rather than offset up-left of it as in the source, and sits close to the plot top edge.
evaluation.notes: A highly recognizable and well-labeled reproduction of the H₂O p–T diagram with an unusually rich and pedagogically apt interaction set (two sliders, heating-path selector, animated heating, 6-step guided demo, drag/click explainers); main weaknesses are an over-exaggerated left lean of the fusion curve, a slightly flattened vaporization curve, and extra tint/state-marker chrome present in the default frame.
action_items: Reduce the melting-curve lean so it is nearly vertical with only a small leftward tilt (matching the source), keeping the negative slope pedagogically visible but not dominant.
Clip or retarget the sublimation curve so it terminates exactly at the axis corner and never crosses the drawn x- or y-axis lines.
Make the region tint and state marker appear only after the user interacts (or at very low opacity) so the step-0 frame matches the plain source figure.

Reshape the vaporization curve so it rises smoothly and convexly from the triple point through (100 °C, 1 atm) to the critical point instead of flattening along the 1 atm guide, and nudge 'Critical point' up-left of the dot as in the source.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are sound; remaining issues are concrete rendering details (curve shapes, clipping at axes, default-frame tint/marker, label offset) that belong to the generator.

plan.concept: The pressure–temperature phase diagram of water: the coexistence curves divide p–T space into solid, liquid, and vapor regions, so a substance's phase is fixed entirely by where its state point sits relative to those curves.
elements: Title 'H2O' centered above the plot
Vertical axis with arrowhead labeled 'Pressure, p (atm)' with nonlinear (quasi-logarithmic) ticks at 0.006, 1, and 218
Horizontal axis with arrowhead labeled 'Temperature, T (°C)' with nonlinear ticks at 0, 0.01, 100, and 374
Red fusion (melting) curve: rises nearly vertically from the triple point, leaning slightly LEFT (negative slope), off the top of the plot
Red vaporization (boiling) curve: sweeps up and right from the triple point to the critical point
Red sublimation curve: continues from the triple point down and left toward the origin corner
Filled black dot at the triple point (0.01 °C, 0.006 atm) with label 'Triple point'
Filled black dot at the critical point (374 °C, 218 atm) with label 'Critical point'
Dashed guide lines from the triple point to both axes (to 0.006 atm and to 0.01 °C)
Dashed guide lines from the critical point to both axes (to 218 atm and to 374 °C)
Dashed guide lines marking the 1 atm / 100 °C crossing on the vaporization curve
Italic region labels: 's' (solid, upper-left region), 'l' (liquid, wedge between melting and boiling curves), 'v' (vapor, lower-right region)
Curved arrow annotations labeled 'Melting', 'Boiling', and 'Sublimation' pointing at the three red branches
Movable state-point marker (open circle) with a live readout of T, p and current phase
Highlight shading for whichever region the state point occupies
Horizontal dashed path line with arrow for the selected heating path (1 atm, low-pressure, supercritical)

interactions.teaches: Moving horizontally across the diagram at fixed pressure crosses coexistence curves and changes the phase — the same substance is ice, water, or steam depending only on where it lands.
interactions.label: Temperature T (°C)

interactions.teaches: Pressure alone can change the phase: raising p at fixed T can cross the melting curve (solid → liquid) or the vaporization curve (vapor → liquid).
interactions.label: Pressure p (atm)

interactions.teaches: Which transitions a substance undergoes depends on the path through p–T space: at 1 atm ice melts then boils, below the triple-point pressure ice sublimates directly to vapor, and above the critical pressure no boundary is crossed at all.
interactions.label: Heating path

interactions.teaches: Watching the state point sweep left to right along a fixed-pressure line makes the boundary crossings — and their absence above the critical point — appear as discrete events.
interactions.label: Heat the sample along the selected path

demo_steps.title: Read the map
demo_steps.narration: Three red curves carve the plane into solid (s), liquid (l), and vapor (v). The state point sits at room conditions, 25 °C and 1 atm, inside the liquid wedge — water is liquid there for no other reason than its location on this map.

demo_steps.title: Cross the boiling curve
demo_steps.narration: Slide the temperature right at 1 atm. At 100 °C the point crosses the vaporization curve and the highlighted region flips from liquid to vapor — that crossing is boiling.

demo_steps.title: The triple point
demo_steps.narration: Drop the pressure to 0.006 atm and the temperature to 0.01 °C. All three curves meet at this single dot, the one condition where ice, water, and steam coexist.

demo_steps.title: Squeeze ice into water
demo_steps.narration: Park the temperature just below 0 °C in the solid region and raise the pressure. Because water's melting curve leans LEFT, climbing vertically eventually crosses it and the label changes from solid to liquid — pressure alone melts ice.

demo_steps.title: Sublimation path
demo_steps.narration: Choose the low-pressure path, below the triple-point pressure, and heat. The point crosses only the sublimation curve: ice turns straight into vapor with no liquid stage.

demo_steps.title: Past the critical point
demo_steps.narration: Now take the supercritical path above 218 atm and heat past 374 °C. No curve is crossed — liquid and vapor merge continuously into one indistinguishable supercritical fluid.

plan.keyInsight: Phase isn't a property you carry with you — it's a location: the state point's position relative to the coexistence curves decides everything, which is why water's uniquely left-leaning melting line lets pressure alone turn ice into liquid.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Single quadrant plot with arrow-tipped axes, white background, black axes and text, the three coexistence curves drawn as one continuous red stroke (~2px). Both axes are strongly nonlinear (log-like) so that 0.006, 1 and 218 atm, and 0, 0.01, 100 and 374 °C, are all comfortably separated; ticks are labeled only at those values. From the triple-point dot (low-left-center) one branch rises steeply and tilts slightly leftward toward the top of the frame (exaggerate the negative slope so it reads clearly), another sweeps up-and-right with increasing steepness to the critical-point dot at the upper right, and a third continues down-left to near the origin. Both special points are filled black dots with plain text labels beside them. Thin black dashed guides run from each special point and from the 1 atm/100 °C crossing to the axes. Italic single-letter region labels s (upper left), l (wedge between the two upper branches), v (lower right). Curved black arrows on the outside of the frame tag 'Melting' (left, pointing at the fusion curve), 'Boiling' (right, pointing at the vaporization curve), and 'Sublimation' (lower left). Interactive additions: a translucent fill tinting the currently occupied region (blue-grey for solid, blue for liquid, warm yellow for vapor, purple wash beyond the critical point), a prominent open-circle state marker with a small readout box showing T, p and the phase name, and when a heating path is selected a horizontal dashed arrow across the plot at that pressure with small tick marks and labels at each boundary crossing ('melting', 'boiling', 'sublimation', or 'no transition').

discrepancies: A faint ghosted state-point marker sits at 25 °C / 1 atm inside the liquid region in the default view — this circle does not exist in the source figure and reads as a stray dot next to the 1 atm guide line.

Red curve hue is slightly brighter/more saturated than the muted crimson of the source, and stroke weight is marginally heavier.
evaluation.notes: An excellent, near drop-in reproduction of the H2O phase diagram — correct curve topology, schematic compressed axes, region letters, special points, dashed guides and leader-arrow annotations — backed by genuinely pedagogical interactions (T/p sliders, heating-path selector with animated traversal, 6-step guided demo, draggable state point, curve popups); only small blemishes remain (extra ghost marker in the default state, critical-point label on the wrong side of its dot).
action_items: Hide the state-point marker entirely at step 0 (alpha 0) so the default view is pixel-faithful to the static source, revealing it only after the first slider/drag/step interaction.
Move the 'Critical point' text so it starts just right of the critical dot (as in the source) rather than straddling/left of it.
Extend the fusion curve slightly higher (closer to the p-axis arrow) and soften the red to the source's crimson (~#d9403c at ~1.8px) for a closer colour/proportion match.
Make the disabled Pressure slider visually obvious (greyed label/track) when a fixed heating path is selected, so students are not confused when it stops responding.
